newsitem.title: USA: Corn prices fall as rains boost crop outlook.
newsitem.headline: Corn prices fall as rains boost crop outlook.

text.p: Corn prices fell on Monday as rain soaked key growing areas in the U.S. Midwest, boosting prospects for this year's crop.
"The rains over the weekend, calls for more in the next few days and rain for this weekend drove it sharply lower," a corn trader on the Chicago Board of Trade said.

Dry soils in parts of the Midwest, especially in central and western Illinois, had been keeping the market on edge. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported on Monday that crop conditions declined last week.
"In our estimation, the dry area of central Illinois is a heck of a lot smaller than it was Friday," said Craig Solberg, meteorologist with Freese-Notis.
CBOT corn for September delivery closed 7-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.45-1/4 a bushel after falling its 12-cent daily limit to $2.40-1/2.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange lumber futures closed the $10 per thousand board feet limit lower, weakened partly by the absence of any major damage to properties in the southeast United States from Hurricane Danny.

"It is pretty clear that we didn't get a lot of structural damage and it should have very little impact (on lumber demand in the southeast U.S.)," said Neil Schmaedick, analyst with Smith Barney Forest Products.
Schmaedick also noted supplies of lumber for prompt delivery were currently plentiful and mills would need to cut prices to stimulate some demand.
"The distribution network is extremely full right now and it is becoming more and more clear that prices are going to have to come down to generate any buying interest," he said.
CME lumber for September delivery closed $10 per thousand board feet lower at $351.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange crude oil futures closed lower, sagging under losses in gasoline prices and a possible surge in Iraqi oil exports once that country's oil-for-food deal with the U.N. restarts.

"Iraq was definitely a factor today, but the market has been anticipating the Iraqi news for a week or two. Gasoline, however, influenced crude to a larger extent," said John Saucer, an analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.
August crude ended nine cents a barrel off at $19.18. August gasoline settled off 0.01 cent a gallon at 60.04 cents while August heating oil finished 0.13 cent up at 52.35 cents a gallon.
The United Nations in Baghdad on Monday said Iraq had submitted a new aid distribution plan, the terms of which have been agreed with U.N. officials, to U.N. headquarters in New York.
Iraq insisted that a new aid distribution plan be approved by the U.N. before the second six months of the oil-for-food deal resumes.
The plan must now receive final approval from the U.N. Secretary-General, and Iraq must submit an oil pricing formula before Iraqi oil sales resume.
The process of putting a new plan in place has delayed the deal's restart since June 8.

Iraq will have to sell more oil in a shorter period of time to meet its $1 billion limit by September. This could mean exports well in excess of 1.5 million barrels a day in August and early September, at least twice the rate Iraq's oil minister recently forecast.
August gasoline, meanwhile, fell as much as 1.20 cents although losses were severely trimmed by the close.
At the Coffee, Cocoa and Sugar Exchange in New York, cocoa prices dropped sharply to a six-week low on heavy speculative selling.
Talk that the outlook for the cocoa crop in the Ivory Coast, the world's leading producer, was improving weighed on the market.
"I think the (Ivorian) new crop is looking better than first expected," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast.

Although Prendergast said the release of the next round of crop estimates was some three weeks away, Ivorian crop analysts and regional buyers said on Monday that the country's 1997/98 cocoa crop was developing strongly, with large harvests possible if favorable weather continues into August.
Cocoa for September delivery ended down $36 per tonne, at $1,504, its lowest settlement since June 10.
